summary:
Karachay-Cherkessia stands under the national framework of Russia, where legal gender recognition has been prohibited outright since President Vladimir Putin signed the law in 2023. The statute bans gender reassignment surgery, forbids any change of gender marker on official documents, voids a marriage concluded by a trans person with someone of their same birth sex, and strips the right to adopt from people diagnosed with gender dysphoria. A visitor presenting documents whose marker does not match their presentation has no lawful route to resolve the discrepancy inside the country.

Public expression is constrained by the propaganda statutes. The 2013 law addressed material concerning minors and was expanded in December 2022 to cover all age groups, reaching content that promotes "non-traditional" sexual relationships, makes minors interested in gender transition, gives minors a "desence to change their sex", or justifies gender transition. Enforcement has accelerated: more than 180 cases were brought under the provisions in 2023 alone, exceeding the total for 2013 to 2022 combined and producing roughly 26 million rubles in fines; cases have risen eighteenfold over the past decade, and fines brought over 60 million rubles into the state budget in the two years to mid-2025.

Since the Supreme Court's November 2023 designation of a non-existent "international LGBT movement" as extremist, displaying the rainbow flag or its colours has drawn charges. Within 48 hours of the ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, with at least two further venues raided the same night. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions as of 30 June 2025, drawn from both the administrative and criminal codes, and between March and May 2026 nine LGBTQ organisations, among them the Russian LGBT Network, Coming Out and Centre T, were outlawed as extremist. In December 2024 a man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel business was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

The North Caucasus, including Karachay-Cherkessia, is treated as worse than the national baseline. The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (version 2.0, June 2025) singles out the North Caucasus as the exception to its otherwise non-persecutory finding on Russia: trans people and public LGBT+ advocates there are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, with systematic regional campaigns documented across 2017 to 2024. The same note records that the 2023 extremist designation carries 2 to 6 years' imprisonment, rising to 6 to 10 years for organising. David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS, an on-the-ground defender now in exile, states that there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus and that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families; he reports year-on-year deterioration across the North Caucasus republics, which include Karachay-Cherkessia.

Coercive conversion practice against trans people is documented. In summer 2021 a transgender woman was lured by relatives to a centre near Novosibirsk and held for nine months, forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour, escaping only after police responded to a phone she had found.

Russia provides no anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, does not designate hate crimes as such, does not treat gender-identity or sexual-orientation motivation as an aggravating factor in sentencing, and does not officially record hate crimes against the LGBTQ community. The 2024 law banning adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that permit gender transitions bears on foreign visitors with residence status.

Entry and onward-protection context: the US State Department advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and includes language relevant to LGBT travellers, and the UK Home Office note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, setting the assessment standard for UK asylum claims. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation, and official national government warnings state this directly to LGBT travellers.
tangentialFactors:
The regional picture separates Karachay-Cherkessia from the rest of Russia in a way that affects both risk assessment and asylum claims. The UK Home Office's June 2025 policy note otherwise finds Russia non-persecutory for LGBT+ people, yet carves out the North Caucasus as an exception where persecution is likely; the same note treats LGBT+ Russians generally as a particular social group for refugee purposes, with Chechnya named explicitly alongside the wider region.

The scale of the national crackdown provides the backdrop. Human Rights Watch counted 101 extremism-related convictions by 30 June 2025, nine LGBTQ organisations were banned as extremist between March and May 2026, and propaganda-case fines exceeded 60 million rubles in the two years to mid-2025. Over 180 propaganda cases in 2023 surpassed the entire 2013 to 2022 total.

Travel advisours state the risk plainly. The US Level 4 Do Not Travel advisory carries explicit language for LGBT travellers, and David Isteev's testimony to the Human Rights House Foundation describes deterioration year on year across the North Caucasus republics, with even private existence capable of prompting violence, detention or forced return to families.

Residents diagnosed with gender dysphoria additionally fall under the 2024 adoption ban framework, and no anti-discrimination protection, hate-crime designation or sentencing aggravation exists on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory does not document how Karachay-Cherkessia's own police, courts or migration authorities handle trans visitors specifically; regional findings are attributed to the North Caucasus as a whole through David Isteev's testimony and the UK Home Office policy note, and no republic-level enforcement data for Karachay-Cherkessia itself is sourced here.

The 2 to 6 and 6 to 10 year imprisonment figures attached to the 2023 extremist designation are as characterised in the UK Home Office June 2025 note; the underlying Russian sentencing provisions are not reproduced in the inventory.

Whether the 2024 law banning adoption by citizens or permanent residents of countries permitting gender transitions affects short-term visitors without residence status is unresolved; the inventory states only that the rule bears on foreign visitors in the country.

No sourced information covers airport or border document screening practices that might out a trans traveller, or access to hormone therapy and other gender-affirming care for foreigners inside Russia. The death of the man detained in a pretrial detention facility in December 2024 is reported without a stated cause.
